This relatively short incubation phase is followed by a rapid nestling period, during which the altricial chicks are brooded intensively by both parents. Chicks are capable of leaving the nest within a few days of hatching but remain dependent on parental provisioning for an extended duration. The initial mass of the hatchling, a mere 55 grams, is substantially lower than the ultimate adult body sizes attained by either sex, indicating a steep growth trajectory during the subsequent weeks of development.

These asymptotic masses are attained gradually, with the most rapid growth occurring during the first two months post-hatching when food delivery from parents is at its peak.

The daily metabolizable energy intake of a 25-day-old chick, which represents the energy ingested minus that lost through excretion, has been measured at 1214 kJ per day  at a body temperature of 39.3 °C [T = 39.3 °C]. This elevated energy demand reflects the high costs of rapid tissue synthesis and thermoregulation in the growing nestling. The total cumulative food energy required from hatching to fledging at 25 days is estimated at 58.6 megajoules , an investment that underscores the substantial parental effort necessary to rear a single offspring to independence. This extended lifespan, which is considerable for a bird of its body size, is characteristic of species with low annual reproductive output and high parental investment. The combination of a long lifespan, infrequent breeding events, and high per-offspring investment in cumulative food energy positions Gavia stellata as a classic slow life-history strategist among waterbirds.
